# Numerical Investigation of Barrett-Crane Models of Riemannian Quantum Gravity

## Introduction and Motivation

The Barrett-Crane model represents one of the most significant proposals for a spin foam formulation of quantum gravity. Emerging from the broader program of loop quantum gravity and topological quantum field theory, these models attempt to provide a background-independent, non-perturbative description of quantum spacetime. In the Riemannian setting, where the underlying symmetry group is SO(4) rather than the Lorentzian SO(3,1), the Barrett-Crane models offer a tractable arena in which the mathematical and physical properties of spin foam quantum gravity can be studied concretely.

Despite their theoretical appeal, the practical computation of physical quantities within these models has remained challenging. The partition functions and observable expectation values are expressed as complicated sums over representations and intertwiners assigned to the elements of a simplicial complex. Analytical evaluation is typically intractable, making numerical methods essential for extracting concrete predictions and understanding the qualitative behavior of the theory.

## Extending the Computational Framework

In this work, we undertake a systematic numerical investigation of the Barrett-Crane models. Our approach builds upon and substantially extends existing computational techniques that were previously limited in scope. Two principal generalizations are introduced.

First, we extend the computational machinery to accommodate **q-deformed models**. The q-deformation replaces the classical group SO(4) with its quantum group counterpart, characterized by a deformation parameter q. When q is taken to be a root of unity, the representation theory becomes truncated, yielding a finite sum in the partition function and effectively introducing a natural infrared cutoff associated with a positive cosmological constant. This regularization is physically significant, as it renders otherwise divergent quantities finite and well-defined.

Second, we generalize our algorithms to handle **arbitrary spacetime triangulations**, rather than being restricted to a small number of highly symmetric or particularly simple simplicial complexes. This flexibility is crucial for probing whether the qualitative features of the models are robust under changes in the underlying discretization, and for approaching questions of triangulation-independence that bear on the continuum limit.

## Observables and Computations

For each model considered, we compute the expectation values of a carefully selected set of observables. These include geometric quantities associated with the areas of triangles and other elementary geometric data encoded in the representation labels. Of particular interest is a **spin-spin correlation function**, which measures the statistical correlation between the representation labels assigned to different faces of the triangulation. Such correlation functions are especially valuable because they probe the propagation of geometric information across the simplicial complex and provide a window into whether the model exhibits long-range order or, conversely, rapidly decaying correlations characteristic of a disordered phase.

By computing these observables across a range of deformation parameters and triangulations, we are able to map out the behavior of the models in a systematic fashion, comparing the undeformed (q = 1) case with the q-deformed variants.

## The Principal Result: Discontinuity of the Limit

The central and most striking finding of our analysis concerns the behavior of the models as the deformation parameter q approaches unity through roots of unity. Naively, one might expect the q-deformed models to reduce smoothly to the undeformed Barrett-Crane model in this limit, recovering the classical SO(4) theory as the deformation is switched off.

Contrary to this expectation, our numerical results reveal that **the limit is discontinuous**. The expectation values of the observables computed in the q-deformed models do not converge to the corresponding values in the undeformed model as q → 1. Instead, a finite gap persists, indicating that the deformed and undeformed theories are separated by a genuine discontinuity rather than being connected by a smooth deformation.

## Discussion and Implications

This surprising discontinuity carries important implications for the interpretation of the Barrett-Crane models. It suggests that the q-deformation is not merely a technical regularization that can be trivially removed, but rather that it fundamentally alters the physical content of the theory. The presence of the cosmological constant introduced through the deformation may therefore have non-trivial and non-perturbative consequences that survive even in the limit of vanishing deformation.

From a broader perspective, these findings underscore the necessity of careful numerical and conceptual scrutiny when interpreting spin foam models. The behavior observed here offers new insight into the structure of these theories and highlights that intuitions borrowed from smooth, classical limits may fail in the quantum gravitational context. Understanding the origin of this discontinuity—whether it reflects a genuine physical phenomenon, a phase transition, or a subtlety in the definition of the models—remains an important direction for future research.

# The Barrett-Crane Model and Riemannian Quantum Gravity

## Introduction

The Barrett-Crane model, introduced by John Barrett and Louis Crane in 1998, represents one of the most influential proposals in the field of spin foam models—a covariant approach to quantum gravity. Originally formulated in the **Riemannian** setting, this model provides a concrete framework for describing quantum spacetime geometry in a background-independent manner.

## Background and Motivation

Spin foam models arose from attempts to give a path-integral formulation to loop quantum gravity. The central idea is to describe the quantum evolution of spin networks—graphs labeled by representations of a symmetry group—through two-dimensional structures called *spin foams*. Barrett and Crane sought to construct such a model for four-dimensional gravity by discretizing spacetime and assigning quantum amplitudes to its geometric building blocks.

## The Riemannian Formulation

In the **Riemannian** version of the model, the relevant symmetry group is **SO(4)**, corresponding to the Euclidean signature of spacetime rather than the physical Lorentzian one. This choice simplifies the mathematics considerably, since the representation theory of SO(4) is well understood and factorizes conveniently into two copies of SU(2).

Key features of the Riemannian Barrett-Crane model include:

- **Simplicial decomposition**: Spacetime is triangulated into four-dimensional simplices (4-simplices), whose faces, edges, and vertices carry geometric data.
- **Simplicity constraints**: A crucial ingredient is the imposition of constraints that reduce the topological BF theory to genuine gravity. These constraints select the so-called *simple representations* of SO(4), ensuring that the quantum states correspond to actual geometric configurations.
- **Vertex amplitudes**: Each 4-simplex is assigned an amplitude, historically related to the **10j-symbol**, encoding the quantum geometry of the elementary building block.

## Significance and Legacy

The Barrett-Crane construction demonstrated that a mathematically well-defined, background-independent amplitude for quantum geometry could be built from first principles. The **Riemannian** model served as an essential testing ground, allowing researchers to explore issues of convergence, asymptotic behavior, and geometric interpretation before tackling the more physically relevant Lorentzian case, which Barrett and Crane addressed in later work.

Although subsequent developments—most notably the EPRL (Engle-Pereira-Rovelli-Livine) and FK (Freidel-Krasnov) models—refined and, in some respects, superseded the original proposal, the Barrett-Crane model remains a landmark. It established many of the conceptual and technical foundations upon which modern spin foam quantum gravity continues to build.

## Conclusion

The work of **Barrett** and **Crane** on the **Riemannian** spin foam model stands as a pivotal contribution to non-perturbative quantum gravity. By translating the geometry of curved spacetime into the language of group representation theory, it opened a productive avenue of research that continues to shape our understanding of the quantum structure of space and time.

Despite its theoretical appeal, the analytic evaluation of these amplitudes remains intractable beyond the simplest configurations, motivating a systematic computational approach.

In this work, we develop efficient algorithms for evaluating the 10j-symbols and associated vertex amplitudes that constitute the fundamental building blocks of the model. Using both direct summation and stationary-phase techniques, we compute spin foam amplitudes for a range of triangulations and analyze their asymptotic behavior in the limit of large spins. These numerical studies clarify several structural features of the Barrett-Crane model, including the dominance of non-geometric configurations that has implications for the recovery of a semiclassical continuum limit. We discuss the consequences of our findings for the viability of the model as a candidate theory of quantum gravity and compare our results with more recent EPRL/FK spin foam constructions. Our computational framework is readily extensible and provides a foundation for future high-performance investigations of spin foam dynamics.

**Abstract**

The Barrett–Crane model provides a spin foam quantization of Riemannian gravity whose observables are notoriously difficult to evaluate beyond the simplest boundary configurations, owing to the noncompact integrations over the space of simple representations of $\mathrm{Spin}(4)$ and the rapid proliferation of amplitude terms with triangulation size. We introduce a suite of numerical techniques for computing gauge-invariant observables in both the classical and the quantum-group-deformed ($q$-deformed) Riemannian Barrett–Crane models. Our approach combines a recursive tensor-network contraction of the vertex amplitudes with an adaptive importance-sampling scheme tailored to the peaked structure of the $\{10j\}$-symbols, together with high-precision evaluation of the balanced $\mathrm{SU}(2)_q \times \mathrm{SU}(2)_q$ intertwiners via stable recurrence relations for $q$-deformed $6j$-symbols. This permits the controlled computation of partition functions, boundary state expectation values, and two-point correlators on triangulations substantially larger than those previously accessible, with quantifiable error bounds.

Applying these methods across a range of deformation parameters $q = e^{i\pi/r}$, we track the behaviour of representative observables as $q \to 1$ (equivalently $r \to \infty$), the limit in which the regularizing cosmological constant is sent to zero and the undeformed model is nominally recovered. We report evidence for a **discontinuous limit**: several observables, including normalized vertex expectation values and the effective boundary correlation length, approach values as $q \to 1^{-}$ that differ sharply from those computed directly in the undeformed model. The discontinuity persists under refinement and is robust against changes in the sampling protocol, indicating that it reflects a genuine feature of the amplitude rather than a numerical artefact. We interpret this behaviour as a manifestation of the noncompactness restored in the $q \to 1$ limit, wherein the deformation acts as a singular rather than a smooth regulator, and we discuss its implications for the continuum limit and for the physical interpretation of the cosmological constant in spin foam quantum gravity.
